Multi-Round Meta-Learning for Label Purification Without Trusted
Labels
Mitsuyoshi Otsu, Jun Zhou, Bo Han, Shirui Pan
Abstract—Label noise remains a fundamental challenge in
supervised deep learning, particularly as modern neural networks
rely on large-scale datasets that frequently suffer from annotation
errors due to cost and scalability constraints. While prior
approaches address this issue through collaborative training
on fully noisy data or meta-learning with access to a small
clean subset, the paradigm of clean-label-free label purification
remains insufficiently explored, which is particularly critical in
expert-annotated domains such as remote sensing and medical
imaging, where annotation inconsistencies persist even among
trained experts. In this work, we propose a clean-label-free
meta-learning framework for label purification. Our approach
introduces a multi-round purification strategy that iteratively
refines label quality by alternating between base-model training
and meta-purification in a decoupled manner, thereby preserving
training stability. We further analyze the multi-round purification
process under a stochastic contraction perspective and introduce
a KL-divergence–based stopping criterion to adaptively select the
purification depth. As a result, our framework enables flexible
downstream training without reliance on complex noisy-label
learning pipelines. Moreover, it captures uncertainty through
accumulated label distributions across rounds, improving the reli-
ability of mislabeled instance detection and correction. Extensive
experiments on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR and mini-
Clothing-1M, show that our method consistently outperforms
state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, it achieves up to a 62.61%
label accuracy improvement on expert-annotated remote sensing
datasets (UC Merced and AID), demonstrating its robustness
in real-world, noise-prone environments. The source code is
available at https://github.com/mitsuyoshiohtsu/MRMP.
Index Terms—Noisy label learning, label purification, meta-
learning, generalization bound, early stopping, remote sensing
I. INTRODUCTION
Supervised deep learning has achieved remarkable success
across various domains, but its effectiveness hinges on the
availability of large volumes of high-quality labeled data. In
practice, however, obtaining accurately annotated datasets at
scale is often infeasible [1], leading to the adoption of more
scalable but error-prone labeling strategies such as crowd-
sourcing and web scraping [2]. These methods introduce
label noise, which can significantly degrade generalization
performance. In particular, deep networks are prone to memo-
rization [3], whereby they eventually fit even incorrect labels,
causing a substantial drop in test accuracy.
To address this issue, learning with noisy labels (LNL) has
emerged as an active research area. Early methods focused
on robust loss functions [4], [5] and noise transition matrix

struggle with scalability and accuracy, especially in large-

such as MentorNet [9] and Co-teaching [10] were proposed to
prioritize small-loss instances during training. These methods
inspired more sophisticated frameworks like DivideMix [11],
which combines semi-supervised learning with consistency
regularization, and ProMix [12], which improves pseudo-label
quality through progressive re-optimization and confidence-
weighted label refinement.
Despite their success, most existing methods rely on heuris-
tic small-loss criteria or ensemble-based architectures [10]–
[14], which increase computational cost and may exacer-
bate confirmation bias. Furthermore, data refinement mech-
anisms—such as instance filtering or pseudo-labeling—are
typically embedded as implicit components of the training
pipeline [15]–[19], making it difficult to evaluate whether the
corrected labels align with human perception or annotation
standards.
Another important line of research explores dynamic label
correction based on model predictions. One of the earliest
methods, Bootstrapping [20], mitigates label noise by lin-
early combining model predictions with the original labels.
Building on this idea, meta-learning approaches such as Meta-
Weight-Net [21], Learning to Reweight Examples [22], and
Meta Label Correction [23] introduce mechanisms to learn
sample weights or correction strategies using a small set of
clean validation labels. More recent frameworks, including
MetaSLC [24], DMLP [25], and L2B [26], further improve
label quality through progressive meta-optimization.
Despite their effectiveness, existing meta-learning methods
still rely on clean validation data, which limits their scalability
in real-world scenarios. An early attempt to overcome this
dependency is PENCIL [27], which integrates label optimiza-
tion directly into the training objective and achieves moderate
improvements without clean supervision. This approach to
noisy label purification has gained renewed attention with the
emergence of the data-centric AI paradigm [28], which em-
phasizes label quality and noise mitigation as core principles
of robust model development.
These challenges are particularly acute in domains such
as medical imaging and remote sensing [29]–[31], where
annotations are costly, difficult to validate, and often incon-
sistent even among experts. However, discussions within the
data-centric community have primarily focused on efficient
data creation pipelines involving human-in-the-loop processes,
rather than on machine learning methodologies capable of
achieving downstream performance comparable to model-
centric noise-robust learning approaches.

In this paper, we propose a clean-label-free label purification
framework based on multi-round meta-learning. Motivated
by the observation that noisy-label learning often imposes
additional constraints on model training, we adopt a decou-
pled formulation by structuring the learning process into two
stages: (1) label cleaning and (2) model optimization. This
separation allows label refinement to proceed independently
of downstream training, enabling a more flexible and model-
agnostic learning paradigm. Our framework focuses on the
first stage, aiming to improve label quality prior to training
the final model.
In each purification round, we randomly sample a meta-
dataset and refine labels by optimizing their alignment with
model performance on the held-out meta-set, as illustrated
in Fig. 1. The refinement is guided by a model trained on
the corresponding base dataset. To improve efficiency, we
fine-tune a pre-trained model and perform lightweight meta-
optimization, thereby avoiding the overhead of full meta-
training. This purification process is repeated iteratively across
multiple rounds.
To mitigate overfitting and confirmation bias over rounds,
we introduce an early stopping criterion based on purification
dynamics—an indicator that captures the stability and pro-
gression of label improvements. This criterion is theoretically
grounded in a stochastic contraction analysis, which character-
izes convergence behavior and provides a principled stopping
rule when further refinement may degrade generalization.
We evaluate our framework on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-
100 with synthetic noise, mini-Clothing-1M with real-world
noise, and two expert-annotated remote sensing datasets (UC
Merced and AID). Experimental results show that our method
significantly improves label quality and model performance
without requiring clean labels. Compared to prior noisy-label
learning and meta-learning-based purification methods, our
approach consistently achieves lower correction error and
superior robustness across diverse datasets.
The key contributions of this work are summarized as
follows:
• We propose a novel clean-label-free label purification
framework based on multi-round meta-learning, which
progressively refines noisy labels without requiring clean
validation data or ensemble-based architectures.
• We leverage high-performance pre-trained models and
adopt scalable meta-learning strategies, enabling efficient
label refinement with standard-scale neural networks.
• We introduce an early stopping criterion based on purifi-
cation dynamics and provide theoretical justification via a
stochastic contraction analysis, which guides the selection
of the optimal number of refinement rounds.
• We conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and
real-world noisy datasets, demonstrating that our method
consistently outperforms or matches state-of-the-art base-
lines, particularly on expert-annotated remote sensing
benchmarks.
• In addition, further experiments show that our framework
produces uncertainty-aware label distributions, which can
assist human rechecking and support additional refine-
ment when necessary.
II. RELATED WORK
Training deep neural networks with noisy labels remains
a significant challenge, as deep models tend to memorize
incorrect labels during the later stages of training [3]. Various
strategies have been developed to address this issue, including
robust training procedures and data purification techniques.
A. Learning with Noisy Labels
As a pioneering approach, MentorNet [9] introduced
curriculum-based sample selection by training a mentor net-
work to weight training samples according to their difficulty.

bias. Co-teaching+ [32] further improves sample diversity by
explicitly encouraging prediction disagreement between the
two networks, reducing the risk of confirmation bias caused

As a combination of co-training and semi-supervised learn-
ing, DivideMix [11] advances noisy-label learning by mod-
eling per-sample losses using a Gaussian Mixture Model
(GMM). It treats low-loss samples as labeled and high-loss
samples as unlabeled, and trains two networks collaboratively
using MixUp [33]. While DivideMix achieves strong per-
formance, it introduces considerable training complexity and
relies heavily on accurate loss modeling. ProMix [12] extends
DivideMix by progressively reweighting pseudo-labels based
on prediction consistency across epochs, thereby improving
label reliability without explicitly partitioning samples into la-
beled and unlabeled sets. This progressive refinement strategy
reduces sensitivity to early-stage prediction errors.
From a different perspective, pseudo-labeling strategies
aim to refine noisy annotations throughout training. Boot-
strapping [20] stabilizes supervision by interpolating between
ground-truth labels and model predictions, while PENCIL [27]
treats labels as optimization variables that are updated jointly
with model parameters. ELR [18] mitigates overfitting to noisy
labels by enforcing consistency between current predictions
and an exponential moving average of historical outputs.
However, confidence-based update mechanisms remain vul-
nerable under high-noise regimes, where prediction certainty
is inherently unreliable.
B. Meta-Learning-Based Label Purification
Meta-learning approaches adapt sample importance or la-
bel correction functions dynamically to improve robustness
against label noise. L2RW [22] learns per-sample weights by
minimizing the meta-validation loss on a small clean dataset,
while Meta-Weight-Net [21] parameterizes a weighting func-
tion based on training losses and optimizes it via meta-
gradients. Meta Label Correction (MLC) [34] extends these
ideas by learning a separate label correction network through
bi-level optimization. Although effective, these methods rely
on clean validation sets and incur significant computational
overhead due to nested gradient computations. To reduce
clean data requirements, MLNT [35] simulates noisy meta-
learning episodes to enhance generalization. However, the joint
optimization of representations and labels often destabilizes
training, particularly in high-noise scenarios.
Recent meta-learning-based methods aim to address these
challenges more effectively. The Decoupled Meta Label Pu-
rifier (DMLP) [25] separates feature learning and label cor-
rection into two distinct stages. DMLP first trains a label-
agnostic feature extractor and then refines noisy labels us-
ing a lightweight meta-label corrector. It introduces Intrinsic
Primary Correction (IPC) for global refinement based on
instance similarities and Extrinsic Auxiliary Correction (EAC)
for fine-grained correction of residual errors. This decoupled
structure stabilizes optimization, reduces computational cost,
and improves purification effectiveness without relying on
clean validation sets.
L2B [26] further advances meta-learning-based purification
by jointly reweighting sample labels and instances through a
learned bootstrapping mechanism guided by meta-objectives.
It adapts supervision dynamically during training and lever-
ages a small clean validation set to optimize the reweighting
functions via meta-gradient updates.

Compared to sample selection, pseudo-labeling, and co-
training methods that often filter out uncertain samples, meta-
learning-based label purification approaches—such as DMLP
and L2B—aim to refine all available labels. This strategy
maximizes data utilization and significantly enhances robust-
ness under varying noise conditions. However, most existing
meta-learning methods still require clean validation data and
involve complex gradient-based optimization, which limits
their scalability in practical applications.
III. METHODOLOGY
This section introduces our multi-round meta-purification
framework for learning with noisy labels and presents the
theoretical foundation for optimizing the number of purifica-
tion rounds. The proposed approach iteratively refines noisy
labels by leveraging pseudo-labels predicted by a fine-tuned
model trained on previously refined labels. We first describe
the overall structure of the framework, followed by details
of the noisy meta-learning mechanism used for label cor-
rection. Finally, we present a stochastic contraction analysis
that provides theoretical support for the multi-round process,
including a formulation for determining the optimal number
of refinement rounds.
A. Overall Framework: Multi-Round Meta-Purification
We propose a multi-round meta-purification (MRMP)
framework designed to improve robustness against label noise.
The core idea is to iteratively refine labels through a decoupled
process that separates model training and label correction.
This decoupling offers two main advantages: (1) it prevents
the leakage of noisy information from meta-validation data
into the base model, and (2) it maintains high model per-
formance by avoiding the instability commonly introduced
by bi-level optimization in meta-learning. To further enhance
performance, the framework leverages a high-performance
pre-trained model for initialization, providing strong repre-
sentational capacity. The model’s predictions are then passed
to a meta-network that performs label purification through a
memory-efficient meta-learning strategy.
Each purification round in the MRMP framework comprises
two key stages: (i) fine-tuning the base model to stabilize
predictions using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA),
and (ii) optimizing a meta-network based on EMA-stabilized
predictions via virtual updates of the fixed base model.
In stage (i), the base model is trained on the noisy training
set for the current round, initialized from a high-performance
pre-trained model to ensure strong representational capacity.
Concurrently, an EMA model is updated in parallel to generate
temporally stable predictions, which serve as reference signals
during the subsequent meta-optimization stage.
In stage (ii), the meta-network gϕ is optimized using meta-
gradients computed from the validation loss. During this
process, the base model remains fixed to prevent optimiza-
tion instability caused by noisy pseudo-labels. After meta-
optimization, the refined labels produced by gϕ are used to
update the training set, and the framework proceeds to the next
round with re-initialized model parameters. This two-stage

B. Meta-Purification Process Within Each Round
Each purification round in the proposed MRMP framework
incorporates a meta-learning step to refine noisy training labels
using a disjoint noisy validation set. Unlike conventional
meta-learning methods that assume access to clean validation
data, our approach acknowledges that both the training and
validation sets may contain label noise. This setting necessi-
tates a clean-label-free meta-purification strategy capable of
mitigating confirmation bias throughout the iterative meta-
optimization process.

V. DISCUSSION
This section examines the behavior and effectiveness of the
proposed MRMP framework by analyzing the accumulation of
confirmation bias during the purification process, as well as the
associated uncertainty and its potential utility for real-world
human re-annotation. A detailed analysis of label correction
dynamics is provided in the supplementary material (see
Section S.5).
A. Analysis on Accumulated Confirmation Bias
Fig. 3 presents a comparative analysis of MRMP and
representative noisy-label learning methods on CIFAR-10N
and CIFAR-100N, which contain human-annotated instance-
dependent label noise. The analysis focuses on the accumula-
tion of confirmation bias, quantified using two complementary
metrics: 1) Noise Detection Rate (NDR), defined as the propor-
tion of detected noisy samples (i.e., samples whose labels are
flipped during purification), and 2) Correct Flip Rate (CFR),
defined as the proportion of noise-to-clean corrections among
all corrected samples. While NDR reflects the aggressiveness
of noise detection, CFR directly characterizes the reliability of
label correction and thus serves as an indicator of accumulated
confirmation bias.
Across both datasets, MRMP consistently achieves high
CFR while maintaining a moderate NDR, resulting in com-
parable or superior purified label accuracy (see Section III).
This behavior indicates that MRMP effectively improves data
quality while limiting the accumulation of confirmation bias.
In contrast, several baselines, including DivideMix, ProMix,
and WSC, exhibit strong noise detection capability but rely
on aggressive correction strategies, as evidenced by very
high NDRs accompanied by substantially reduced CFRs. In
particular, on CIFAR-100N, most competing methods achieve
CRF values below 50%, indicating that fewer than half of
the applied label flips align with the underlying clean la-
bels. Such low-precision corrections are prone to amplifying
confirmation bias, posing a serious concern for practical data
purification. By comparison, MRMP consistently maintains a
high CFR, remaining above 75% even under severe noise,
demonstrating reliable correction behavior in realistic noisy
settings. Additional analysis of accumulated confirmation bias
on CIFAR-10/100 is provided in the supplementary material
(see Section S.6).
B. Semi-Automatic Correction on Remote Sensing Datasets
The high Correct Flip Rate (CFR) achieved by MRMP
reflects the strong reliability of its purified datasets, which in
turn enables practical downstream use cases—most notably,
a second-stage human annotation process aimed at further
improving label quality. To make this feasible, an efficient
strategy for identifying potentially erroneous labels is re-
quired, underscoring the importance of uncertainty estimation.
To explore this possibility, Fig. 4 examines the relationship
between model confidence and prediction correctness, along
with simulated correction curves for the UC Merced and
AID datasets under 40% asymmetric noise. Despite moderate
correlation levels (Pearson r ≈0.4 for UC Merced and
r ≈0.3 for AID), the simulated correction process, which
is performed by re-labeling samples in ascending order of
confidence, reveals that correcting only 30% of the least
confident predictions can correct the remaining noisy labels
by around 85% on both datasets. These results support the
feasibility of confidence-guided refinement, especially in do-
mains where acquiring clean supervision is expensive. With its
round-wise, soft-label trajectories and accumulated uncertainty
signals, MRMP provides a robust foundation for enabling
semi-automatic correction pipelines in expert-labeled datasets.

VI. ABLATION STUDY
To assess the contribution of each key component in the
proposed MRML framework, we conduct ablation experiments
on CIFAR-10 and UC Merced under 50% symmetric label
noise, representing general-purpose and expert-annotated noise
scenarios, respectively. Results are summarized in Table V.
Effect of Multi-round Purification: Removing the multi-
round purification process and instead using normalized
single-round predictions for label replacement results in
substantial performance degradation (–7.82% on CIFAR-10,
–15.18% on UC Merced). This confirms that iterative refine-
ment is critical for progressively enhancing label quality and
mitigating abrupt, unstable shifts in supervision.
Effect of KL-based Early Stopping: We disable the KL-
based stopping criterion and fix the purification rounds to 5.
This change causes a moderate decline in accuracy (–2.34% on
CIFAR-10, –0.77% on UC Merced), indicating that adaptive
termination of purification helps avoid both under- and over-
refinement of labels.
Effect of Exponential Moving Average (EMA): Excluding
EMA results in a sharp accuracy drop on CIFAR-10 (–21.52%)
and a moderate decline on UC Merced (–0.77%), underscor-
ing the importance of temporal smoothing. Inspired by the
success of ELR and ELR+ [18], EMA mitigates the gradual
drift of model predictions from clean to noisy by stabilizing
pseudo-labels across purification rounds—an effect that proves
especially beneficial for maintaining robust label updates in
MRMP on CIFAR-10.

Effect of Meta-Learning: Disabling meta-learning and
performing label updates directly on the EMA outputs with a
fixed momentum coefficient (β = 0.2) results in a performance

This confirms that meta-optimization plays a crucial role in
effectively distinguishing clean from noisy samples—even in
the absence of clean validation data.
Effect of Pretraining: Replacing pretrained weights with
random initialization degrades performance to 74.05% on
CIFAR-10 and 62.38% on UC Merced. While the framework
still outperforms the noisy-label baseline, this result under-
scores the importance of pretrained representations in guiding
effective label purification. Without such prior knowledge, the
model becomes more susceptible to the influence of noisy
labels, leading to unstable and suboptimal refinement.
Overall, these results validate the necessity of each com-
ponent in enhancing label reliability and highlight the central
roles of multi-round refinement and meta-learning across both
general-purpose and domain-specific (e.g., remote sensing)
classification tasks.
VII. CONCLUSION
In summary, this work demonstrates the practical potential
of clean-label-free purification through the proposed multi-
round meta-purification (MRMP) framework. MRMP exhibits
strong robustness to label noise across diverse benchmarks,
including CIFAR-10/100, CIFAR-10N/100N, mini-Clothing-
1M, and expert-annotated remote sensing datasets, showing
that decoupling label refinement from model training is an
effective strategy for improving label quality without clean
supervision. Our theoretical analysis motivates a KL-based
stopping criterion that identifies an appropriate refinement
round and is empirically shown to reduce confirmation bias
during label purification. In addition, the evolution of soft
labels provides informative signals for identifying uncertain or
error-prone samples, suggesting potential benefits for human–
AI collaborative annotation.
Several challenges remain for practical implementation.
Improving the scalability and adaptability of MRMP to diverse
real-world datasets, including settings that require training
from scratch or involve large-scale data and higher-capacity
models, is an important direction for future work. Extending
MRMP to multi-label problems and structured prediction
tasks, such as semantic segmentation, also remains open.
Overall, MRMP offers a promising step toward scalable and
practical label purification in scenarios where high-quality
annotations are costly or inconsistently available.
